blocks.text: An office in the royal palace. Two writing-tables face each other from opposite sides of the room, leaving plenty of room between them. Each table has a chair by it for visitors. The door is in the middle of the farthest wall. The clock shows that it is a little past 11; and the light is that of a fine summer morning.
Sempronius, smart and still presentably young, shows his right profile as he sits at one of the tables opening the King’s letters.

Pamphilius, middle aged, shows his left as he leans back in his chair at the other table with a pile of the morning papers at his elbow, reading one of them. This goes on silently for some time. Then Pamphilius, putting down his paper, looks at Sempronius for a moment before speaking.
I don’t mean his religion. I mean his profession. And his politics.
He was a Ritualist by profession, a Ritualist in politics, a Ritualist in religion: a raging emotional Die Hard Ritualist right down to his boots.
Do you mean that he was a parson?

Not at all. He was a sort of spectacular artist. He got up pageants and Lord Mayors’ Shows and military tattoos and big public ceremonies and things like that. He arranged the last two coronations. That was how I got my job here in the palace. All our royal people knew him quite well: he was behind the scenes with them.
Behind the scenes and yet believed they were all real!
Yes. Believed in them with all his soul.
Certainly. Do you suppose a baker cannot believe sincerely in the sacrifice of the Mass or in holy communion because he has baked the consecrated wafer himself?
Did you ever ask him what he really thought about it all? But of course you didn’t: one can’t ask one’s father anything about himself.

My dear Pam: my father never thought. He didn’t know what thought meant. Very few people do, you know. He had vision: actual bodily vision, I mean; and he had an oddly limited sort of imagination. What I mean is that he couldn’t imagine anything he didn’t see; but he could imagine that what he did see was divine and holy and omniscient and omnipotent and eternal and everything that is impossible if only it looked splendid enough, and the organ was solemn enough, or the military bands brassy enough.
You mean that he had to get everything from outside.

Exactly. He’d never have felt anything if he hadn’t had parents to feel about in his childhood, and a wife and babies to feel about when he grew up. He’d never have known anything if he hadn’t been taught at school. He couldn’t amuse himself: he had to pay oceans of money to other people to amuse him with all sorts of ghastly sports and pleasures that would have driven me into a monastery to escape from them. You see it was all ritual: he went to the Riviera every winter just as he went to church.
By the way, is he alive? I should like to know him.
No. He died in 1962, of solitude.
What do you mean? of solitude?
He couldn’t bear to be alone for a moment: it was death to him. Somebody had to be with him always.
Oh well, come! That was friendly and kindly. It shows he had something inside him after all.
Not a bit. He never talked to his friends. He played cards with them. They never exchanged a thought.
He must have been a rum old bird.
Not rum enough to be noticed. There are millions like him.
But what about his dying of solitude? Was he imprisoned?

No. His yacht struck a reef and sank somewhere off the north of Scotland; and he managed to swim to an uninhabited island. All the rest were drowned; and he was not taken off for three weeks. When they found him he was melancholy mad, poor old boy; and he never got over it. Simply from having no one to play cards with, and no church to go to.
My dear Sem: one isn’t alone on an uninhabited island. My mother used to stand me on the table and make me recite about it.

To sit on rocks; to muse o’er flood and fell; To slowly trace the forest’s shady scene Where things that own not man’s dominion dwell And mortal foot hath ne’er or rarely been; To climb the trackless mountain all unseen With the wild flock that never needs a fold; Alone o’er steeps and foaming falls to lean: This is not solitude: ’tis but to hold Converse with Nature’s charms, and view her stores unrolled.

Now you have hit the really funny thing about my father. All that about the lonely woods and the rest of it﻿—what you call Nature﻿—didn’t exist for him. It had to be something artificial to get at him. Nature to him meant nakedness; and nakedness only disgusted him. He wouldn’t look at a horse grazing in a field; but put splendid trappings on it and stick it into a procession and he just loved it. The same with men and women: they were nothing to him until they were dressed up in fancy costumes and painted and wigged and titled. To him the sacredness of the priest was the beauty of his vestment, the loveliness of women the dazzle of their jewels and robes, the charm of the countryside not in its hills and trees, nor in the blue smoke from its cottages in the winter evenings, but of its temples, palaces, mansions, park gates, and porticoed country houses. Think of the horror of that island to him! A void! a place where he was deaf and dumb and blind and lonely! If only there had been a peacock with its tail in full bloom it might have saved his reason; but all the birds were gulls; and gulls are not decorative. Our King could have lived there for thirty years with nothing but his own thoughts. You would have been all right with a fishing rod and a golf ball with a bag of clubs. I should have been as happy as a man in a picture gallery looking at the dawns and sunsets, the changing seasons, the continual miracle of life ever renewing itself. Who could be dull with pools in the rocks to watch? Yet my father, with all that under his nose, was driven mad by its nothingness. They say that where there is nothing the king loses his rights. My father found that where there is nothing a man loses his reason and dies.
Let me add that in this palace, when the king’s letters are not ready for him at 12 o’clock, a secretary loses his job.
Do Orinthia’s letters go to the Queen?
No, by George! Even I don’t read Orinthia’s letters. My instructions are to read everything; but I take care to forget to open hers. And I notice that I am not rebuked for my negligence.
Oh shut up, Pam. I shall never get through if you go on talking.
I was only going to say that I suppose﻿—
Something about Orinthia. Don’t. If you indulge in supposition on that subject, you will lose your job, old chap. So stow it.

Don’t cry out before Orinthia is hurt, young chap. I was going to say that I suppose you know that that bull-roarer Boanerges has just been taken into the Cabinet as President of the Board of Trade, and that he is coming here today to give the King a piece of his mind, or what he calls his mind, about the crisis.

What does the King care about the crisis? There has been a crisis every two months since he came to the throne; but he has always been too clever for them. He’ll turn Boanerges inside out after letting him roar the palace down.
Look here. The King has an appointment with me at a quarter to twelve. How long more am I to be kept waiting?
Shortly, but a little taken aback.
Oh yes: I’ve heard of you. You’re one of the king’s private secretaries.

Well, I told one of them to tell the king I was here, and to look sharp about it. He looked at me as if I was a performing elephant, and took himself off after whispering to another flunkey. Then this other chap comes over to me and pretends he doesn’t know who I am! asks me can he have my name! “My lad,” I said: “not to know me argues yourself unknown. You know who I am as well as I do myself. Go and tell the king I’m waiting for him, d’ye see?” So he took himself off with a flea in his ear. I waited until I was fed up with it, and then opened the nearest door and came in here.
Oh: that was Sempronius, was it. I’ve heard of him too.

You seem to have heard of all of us. You will be quite at home in the palace now that you are a Cabinet Minister. By the way, may I congratulate you on your appointment﻿—or rather congratulate the Cabinet on your accession?
You will allow me to be seated?
Oh, sit down, man, sit down. You’re in your own house: ceremony cuts no ice with me.
Indicating the secretaries with a jerk of his head.
My private secretaries. Do they incommode you?
Oh, they don’t incommode me. I am ready to have our talk out in Trafalgar Square if you like, or have it broadcast on the wireless.
I warn you it won’t be agreeable. I am a plain man, Magnus: a very plain man.
Not at all, I assure you﻿—
Surprised and enormously flattered; he cannot help smiling with pleasure.
Now convinced that he has the upper hand.
I shall be only too grateful to them for taking a very difficult and thankless job off my hands.
But it’s not on your hands. It’s on your ministers’ hands. You are only a constitutional monarch. Do you know what they call that in Belgium?
An india rubber stamp, I think. Am I right?
You are, King Magnus. An india rubber stamp. That’s what you have got to be; and don’t you forget it.
Yes: that’s what we are most of the time: both of us.

They bring us papers. We sign. You have no time to read them, luckily for you. But I am expected to read everything. I do not always agree; but I must sign: there is nothing else to be done. For instance, death warrants. Not only have I to sign the death warrants of persons who in my opinion ought not to be killed; but I may not even issue death warrants for a great many people who in my opinion ought to be killed.

Many men would hardly miss their heads, there is so little in them. Still, killing is a serious business: at least the person who is to be killed is usually conceited enough to think so. I think that if there were a question of killing me﻿—
Oh, quite. I have not forgotten King Charles’s head. Well, I hope it will be settled by a living person and not by an india rubber stamp.
It will be settled by the Home Secretary, your duly constituted democratic minister.
At present, perhaps. But not when I am Home Secretary, by Jingo! Nobody will make an india rubber stamp of Bill Boanerges: take that from me.

Of course not. Is it not curious how people idealize their rulers? In the old days the king﻿—poor man!﻿—was a god, and was actually called God and worshipped as infallible and omniscient. That was monstrous﻿—

But was it half so silly as our pretence that he is an india rubber stamp? The ancient Roman emperor-god had not infinite wisdom, infinite knowledge, infinite power; but he had some: perhaps even as much as his ministers. He was alive, not dead. What man has ever approached either a king or a minister and been able to pick him up from the table and use him as one picks up and uses a piece of wood and brass and rubber? Permanent officials of your department will try to pick you up and use you like that. Nineteen times out of twenty you will have to let them do it, because you cannot know everything; and even if you could you cannot do everything and be everywhere. But what about the twentieth time?
The twentieth time they will find they are up against Bill Boanerges, eh?
A soul, eh? You kings still believe in that, I suppose.
I find the word convenient: it is short and familiar. But if you dislike being called a soul, let us say that you are animate matter as distinguished from inanimate.
And you are up against mine.

It is not for me to make that qualification, except in my own case. Besides, you have given your proofs. No common man could have risen as you have done. As for me, I am a king because I was the nephew of my uncle, and because my two elder brothers died. If I had been the stupidest man in the country I should still be its king. I have not won my position by my merits. If I had been born as you were in the﻿—in the﻿—
In the gutter. Out with it. Picked up by a policeman at the foot of Captain Coram’s statue. Adopted by the policeman’s grandmother, bless her!
Ah! Where? Not, mind you, that you mightn’t have done pretty well for yourself. You’re no fool, Magnus: I will say that for you.
Flatter a king! Never. Not Bill Boanerges.
Yes, yes: everybody flatters the King. But everybody has not your tact, and, may I say? your good nature.
That is what has always surprised me. Do you really think that any man should have as much personal power as the presidents of the republican States have? Ambitious kings envy them.
What’s that? I don’t follow that.
Come come! You know it as well as I do. Well, if it happens you will have ten times more power than I have ever had.

And what is the King? An idol set up by a group of plutocrats so that they can rule the country with the King as their scapegoat and puppet. Presidents, now, are chosen by the people, who always want a Strong Man to protect them against the rich.
Well, speaking as a bit of a Strong Man myself, there may be something in that. But honestly, Magnus, as man to man, do you tell me you’d rather be a president than what you are?
By no means. You wouldn’t believe me if I did; and you would be quite right. You see, my security is very comfortable.
Security, eh? You admitted just now that even a modest individual like myself had given your throne a shake or two.

True. You are quite right to remind me of it. I know that the monarchy may come to an end at any moment. But while the monarchy lasts﻿—while it lasts, mark you﻿—I am very secure. I escape the dreadful and demoralizing drudgery of electioneering. I have no voters to please. Ministers come and ministers go; but I go on forever. The terrible precariousness of your position﻿—
What’s that? How is my position precarious?
The vote may go against you. Yours is a Trade Union seat, is it not? If the Hydroelectric Workers Federation throw you over, where would you be?
Suppose a man with a bigger voice comes along! Some fool! Some windbag! Some upstart with a platform trick of gulling the multitude!
That’s true. But I can talk Iky’s head off.
Lucky man: you have all the trumps in your hand. But I, who cannot pretend to your gifts, am very glad that Iky cannot upset me as long as I am the nephew of my uncle.
Papa: I cannot find the address﻿—
Rising in a glow of gratification.
The uniform of Labor, your Royal Highness. I’m proud of it.
Of course, that makes all the difference.
And the girl hasn’t been spoilt. I was glad to see that. She doesn’t seem to know that she is the Princess Royal, eh?
Well, she wouldn’t dream of giving herself any airs with you.
What! Isn’t she always like that?
Oh no. It’s not everybody who is received as you have been. I hope you have enjoyed your visit.
Well, I pulled Magnus through it pretty well: eh? Don’t you think so?
Well, perhaps I have, perhaps I have.
Where do you think you are?
Who do you think you are?
Turning on them like a baited bear.
Right as rain, Joe. You leave the King to me. I know how to handle him. If I’d been in the Cabinet these last three months there’d have been no crisis.
He put you through it, did he?
What do you mean? put me through it? Is this a police office?
No. But the Princess Alice happened to drop in. She was greatly impressed by the President.
What in hell are you laughing at?

Now to start with, do you chaps all fully realize that though we wiped out every other party at the last election, and have been in power for the last three years, this country has been governed during that time by the King?

The worst of you is that you won’t face the fact that though you’re Prime Minister you’re not God Almighty. The king can’t do anything except what we advise him to do. How can he govern the country if we have all the power and he has none?

Don’t talk silly, Nick. This india rubber stamp theory doesn’t work. What man has ever approached a king or a minister and been able to pick him up from the table and use him as you’d use a bit of wood and brass and rubber? The King’s a live man; and what more are you, with your blessed advice?
Hullo, Bill! You have been having your mind improved by somebody.
What do you mean? Isn’t it what I have always said?
It’s enough to drive a man mad. I am sorry.
Late as usual. Come! Business, business, business.

The King is working the Press against us. The King is making speeches. Things have come to a head. He said yesterday on the opening of the new Chamber of Commerce building that the king’s veto is the only remaining defence of the people against corrupt legislation.
So it is, by Jingo. What other defence is there? Democracy? Yah! We know what Democracy is worth. What we need is a Strong Man.

I should stand a better chance than you, my lad, if we were a Republic, and the people could choose. And let me tell you that a republican president has more power than a king because the people know that they need a Strong Man to protect them against the rich.
Flinging himself back in his chair in desperation.
What! Now! You can’t. You mustn’t.
Of course not. Out of the question.
But not at such a moment as this. Don’t let us swap horses when crossing a stream.
Why not, if the horse you have got is subject to hysterics?
Not to mention that you may have more than one horse at your disposal.
Right you are. Perfectly true. Take my job, Nick. It’s vacant for you, Bill. I wish you joy of it.
Now boys, boys, boys: be good. We can’t make a new Cabinet before Magnus comes in. You have something in your pocket, Joe. Out with it. Read it to them.
Taking a paper from his pocket.
You’re sick already, by your own account. I only ask, suppose he refuses to sign your ultimatum?
You call yourself a Cabinet Minister, and you can’t answer that!
Or we resign and tell the country that we can’t carry on the King’s Government under conditions which destroy our responsibility.
That’ll do it. He couldn’t face that.
I retain an open mind. Let us hear the ultimatum.

I protest. It is intolerable. I call a conference of my Cabinet to consider our position in regard to the prerogative; and I find the two lady members, the Postmistress General and the Powermistress General, closeted with your Majesty instead of being in their places to confer with me.
You mind your own business, Joe.

Oh no: really, really, my dear Lysistrata, you must not take that line. Our business is to meddle in everybody’s business. A Prime Minister is a busybody by profession. So is a monarch. So are we all.
He sits down distractedly, and buries his face in his hands.
Going to him and petting him.
What do you go provoking Lizzie for like that? You know she has a temper.
There is nothing whatever wrong with my temper. But I am not going to stand any of Joe’s nonsense; and the sooner he makes up his mind to that the smoother our proceedings are likely to be.

I protest. I say, let us be dignified. I say, let us respect ourselves and respect the throne. All this Joe and Bill and Nick and Lizzie: we might as well be hobnobbing in a fried fish shop. The Prime Minister is the prime minister: he isn’t Joe. The Powermistress isn’t Lizzie: she’s Lysis Traitor.
Who has evidently been a schoolmistress.
He flings himself into his chair.
Prime Minister: the word is with you. Why have you all simultaneously given me the great pleasure of exercising your constitutional right of access to the sovereign?
Have I that right, sir; or haven’t I?
Oh for Heaven’s sake don’t contradict her, Joe. We shall never get anywhere at this rate. Come to the crisis.
The ultimatum. Lets have the ultimatum.
Your Majesty’s allusion to the royal veto in a speech yesterday has brought matters to a head.

It was perhaps indelicate. But you all allude so freely to your own powers﻿—to the supremacy of Parliament and the voice of the people and so forth﻿—that I fear I have lost any little delicacy I ever possessed. If you may flourish your thunderbolts why may I not shoulder my little popgun of a veto and strut up and down with it for a moment?
This is not a subject for jesting﻿—
Oh please no, your Majesty. We get enough of that from Joe.
Tch-tch-tch! Gently, Amanda, gently. Three very promising lads: they do you credit.
I never wanted them to go to sea. I could have found them better jobs in the Post Office.
Apart from Amanda’s family relations, am I face to face with a united Cabinet.
No, sir. You are face to face with a squabbling Cabinet; but, on the constitutional question, united we stand: divided we fall.
What is the constitutional question? Do you deny the royal veto? or do you object only to my reminding my subjects of its existence?
What we say is that the king has no right to remind his subjects of anything constitutional except by the advice of the Prime Minister, and in words which he has read and approved.
Which Prime Minister? There are so many of them in the Cabinet.

There! Serves you all right! Aren’t you ashamed of yourselves? But I am not surprised, Joseph Proteus. I own I like a Prime Minister that knows how to be a Prime Minister. Why do you let them take the word out of your mouth every time?
If His Majesty wants a Cabinet of dumb dogs he will not get it from my party.
Heaven forbid! The variety of opinion in the Cabinet is always most instructive and interesting. Who is to be its spokesman today?
I know your Majesty’s opinion of me; but let﻿—
He straightens up and becomes impressively eloquent.
I mean that when you disagree with us you are to keep your disagreement to yourself.
That would be a very heavy responsibility for me. If I see you leading the nation over the edge of a precipice may I not warn it?
It is our business to warn it, not yours.
Suppose you don’t do your business! Suppose you don’t see the danger! That has happened. It may happen again.
Rot! It’s happening all the time until somebody has the gumption to put his foot down and stop it.
Yes: I know. But that is not democracy.

Wages are too high, if you ask me. Anybody can earn from five to twenty pounds a week now, and a big dole when there is no job for him. And what Englishman will give his mind to politics as long as he can afford to keep a motor car?
How many voted at the last election? Not seven percent of the register.
Yes; and the seven percent were only a parcel of sillies playing at ins and outs. To make democracy work in Crassus’s way we need poverty and hardship.

No: we have not abolished poverty and hardship. Our big business men have abolished them. But how? By sending our capital abroad to places where poverty and hardship still exist: in other words, where labor is cheap. We live in comfort on the imported profits of that capital. We are all ladies and gentlemen now.
Well, what more do you want?
You surely don’t grudge us our wonderful prosperity, sir.
No: it was the Prime Minister who used those expressions.
There is no need to rub it in like that, Nick. We’re all good friends. Nobody objects to prosperity.
You think this prosperity is safe?

Safe! Look at my constituency: Northeast-by-north Birmingham, with its four square miles of confectionery works! Do you know that in the Christmas cracker trade Birmingham is the workshop of the world?

Take Gateshead and Middlesbrough alone! Do you know that there has not been a day’s unemployment there for five years past, and that their daily output of chocolate creams totals up to twenty thousand tons?
It is certainly a consoling thought that if we were peacefully blockaded by the League of Nations we could live for at least three weeks on our chocolate creams.
You needn’t sneer at the sweets: we turn out plenty of solid stuff. Where will you find the equal of the English golf club?
Look at the potteries: the new crown Derby! the new Chelsea! Look at the tapestries! Why, Greenwich Goblin has chased the French stuff out of the market.
Don’t forget our racing motor boats and cars, sir: the finest on earth, and all individually designed. No cheap mass production stuff there.
And our livestock! Can you beat the English polo pony?
Or the English parlormaid? She wins in all the international beauty shows.
Now Mandy, Mandy! None of your triviality.
I am not sure that the British parlormaid is not the only real asset in your balance sheet.
Well, sir? Are you satisfied that we have the best paid proletariat in the world on our side?
All except the two women laugh uproariously at this.

I must join them there, sir. I am as much against chocolate creams as you are: they never agree with me. But a revolution in England!!! Put that out of your head, sir. Not if you were to tear up Magna Carta in Trafalgar Square, and light the fires of Smithfield to burn every member of the House of Commons.
I was not thinking of a revolution in England. I was thinking of the countries on whose tribute we are living. Suppose it occurs to them to stop paying it! That has happened before.
Oh no, sir: no, no, no. What would become of their foreign trade with us?
At a pinch, I think they could do without the Christmas crackers.
Who has been listening with implacable contempt to the discussion, suddenly breaks in in a sepulchral contralto.
A lie. A flat lie. He is not related to me. He is only my stepson’s father-in-law.

I demand an explanation of the words bungling and squabbling. We have had quite enough of them here today. Who are you getting at? It was not I who bungled the Factory Bill. I found it on my desk when I took office, with all His Majesty’s suggestions in the margin; and you know it.
Have you all done playing straight into His Majesty’s hand, and making my situation here impossible?
You shut up, Bert. It’s true.

Well, what will happen? There will be no denials, no excuses, no vindications. We shall not fall into that trap, clever as you are at setting it. Crassus will say just simply that you are a freethinker. And Balbus will say that you are a libertine.
Now, King Magnus! Our cards are on the table. What have you to say?

Admirably put! People ask how it is that with all these strong characters around you hold your own as the only possible Prime Minister, in spite of your hysterics and tantrums, your secretiveness and your appalling laziness﻿—

I am not a wonderful man. There is not a man or woman here whose job I could do as well as they do it. I am Prime Minister for the same reason that all Prime Ministers have been Prime Ministers: because I am good for nothing else. But I can keep to the point﻿—when it suits me. And I can keep you to the point, sir, whether it suits you or not.
At all events you do not flatter kings. One of them, at least, is grateful to you for that.

Kings, as you and I very well know, rule their ministers by flattering them; and now that you are the only king left in the civilized half of Europe Nature seems to have concentrated in you all the genius for flattery that she used to have to divide between half a dozen kings, three emperors, and a Sultan.
But what interest has a king in flattering a subject?
Suppose she’s a good-looking woman, sir!
Suppose he has a lot of money, and the king’s hard up!
Suppose he is a Prime Minister, and you can do nothing except by his advice.
Well, nothing can be fairer than that.
Ever the best of friends. I am the last to kick a man when he’s down.
I may be a jobber; but nobody shall say that I am an ungenerous opponent.
Suddenly overwhelmed with emotion, rises and begins singing in stentorian tones.
Should auld acquaintance be forgot, And never brought to mind﻿—
Making no further attempt to conceal his merriment.
I don’t understand this, I understood His Majesty to give way to us in, I must say, the handsomest manner. Can’t we take our victory like gentlemen?
Composing her features as best she can.
I hope your Majesty recognizes that kings are not the only people to whom certain sorts of mud always stick, no matter what fool throws them. Call a minister a jobber﻿—

Yes, or a bungler, and everybody believes it. Jobbery and incompetence are the two sorts of mud that stick to us, no matter how honest or capable we are; and we haven’t the royal vantage that you enjoy, that the more the ladies take away your character the better the people like you.
This a free country, Bill. A sense of humor is not a crime. And when the King is not setting me off, you are.
Where is the joke? I don’t see it.
If you could see a joke, Bill, you wouldn’t be the great popular orator you are.
Thank Heaven, I am not a silly giggler like some I could mention.
Thanks, dearest Bill. Now, Joe: don’t you think you have let us run loose long enough? What about that ultimatum?

I am in no hurry. His Majesty’s speeches are very wise and interesting; and your back chat amuses both you and him. But the ultimatum is here all the time; and I shall not leave this room until I have His Majesty’s signed pledge that its conditions will be observed.
What! Not even if you dictate them?
Not even if we dictate them. Your Majesty has a way of unrolling the manuscript and winking﻿—
You know what I mean. The best speech in the world can be read in such a way as to set the audience laughing at it. We have had enough of that. So, in future, no speeches.
Of course we cannot object to such speeches as “We declare this foundation stone well and truly laid” and so forth. But politically, yes: a dumb king.
The working of the Press from the palace back stairs must cease.

You know that I have no control of the Press. The Press is in the hands of men much richer than I, who would not insert a single paragraph against their own interests even if it were signed by my own hand and sent to them with a royal command.

We know that. But though these men are richer than you, they are not cleverer. They get amusing articles, spiced with exclusive backstairs information, that don’t seem to them to have anything to do with politics. The next thing they know is that their pet shares have dropped fifteen points; that capital is frightened off their best prospectuses; and that some of the best measures in our party program are made to look like city jobs.
Am I supposed to write these articles?
Your man Sempronius does. I can spot his fist out of fifty columns.
So can I. When he is getting at me he always begins the sentence with “Singularly enough.”

Is there to be any restriction on the other side? I have noticed, for instance, that in a certain newspaper which loses no opportunity of disparaging the throne, the last sentence of the leading article almost invariably begins with the words “Once for all.” Whose trademark is that?
I know when to be frank. I learnt the trick from Your Majesty.
Joe frank! When I want to find out what he is up to I have to come and ask your Majesty.
That is perfectly true. In this Cabinet there is no such thing as a policy. Every man plays for his own hand.
It’s like a game of cards.

You know quite well what I mean. When will you learn, Nicobar, that it is no use trying to browbeat me. I began life as a schoolmistress; and I can browbeat any man in this Cabinet or out of it if he is fool enough to try to compete with me in that department.
Order! order! Cannot the Prime Minister check these unseemly personalities?
They give me time to think, Bill. When you have had as much parliamentary experience as I have you will be very glad of an interruption occasionally. May I proceed?
His Majesty asks whether the restriction on press campaigning is to be entirely onesided. That, I take it, sir, is your question.
The answer is in the affirmative.
Yes: one thing more. The veto must not be mentioned again. That can apply to both sides, if you like. The veto is dead.
May we not make a historical reference to the corpse?

No. I cannot carry on the King’s government unless I can give pledges and carry them out. What is my pledge worth if our constituents are reminded every day that the King may veto anything that Parliament does? Do you expect me to say, when I am asked for a pledge, “You must ask the King”?
I have to say “You must ask the Prime Minister.”
Quite. I only mention it to show that the Prime Minister does not really wish to kill the veto. He only wishes to move it next door.
The people live next door. The name on the brass plate is Public Opinion.
I doubt if that is any longer true, sir. I know that I get blamed for everything that goes wrong in my department.

Ah! But what a despot you are, Lysistrata! Granted, however, that the people have found out long ago that democracy is humbug, and that instead of establishing responsible government it has abolished it, do you not see what this means?
I think I am in the running. That is why I do not feel bound to accept this ultimatum. By signing it I put myself out of the running. Why should I?
Because you’re the king: that’s why.
If two men ride the same horse, one must ride behind.
With placid but formidable obstinacy and ironical explicitness.
That is exactly the question that has to be settled here and now.
He dashes out of the room.
You’ve done it now, Mandy. I hope you’re proud of yourself.
It is you, Amanda, who should go and coax him back. But I suppose I must do it myself, as usual. Excuse me, ladies and gentlemen.
He rises. The rest rise. He goes out.
He flings himself back into his chair.
What are we to do now? that’s what I want to know.
Sits down with a little splutter of laughter.
He is settling the whole business with the King behind our backs. That is what Joe always contrives to do, by hook or crook.
You didn’t arrange it with him, Mandy: did you?
There wasn’t any need to arrange it. Joe can always depend on one or other of us saying something that will give him an excuse for flying out.

In my opinion, ladies and gentlemen, we have done our bit, and may leave the rest to Joe. Matters had reached a point at which it was yes or no between the Cabinet and the Crown. There is only one sort of committee that is better than a committee of two; and that is a committee of one. Like the family in Wordsworth’s poem, we are seven﻿—
You did speak that piece beautifully, sir.
Booze, my Balby: booze. Raising the elbow!
Mike never knows when to stop.
The time for Mike to stop is before he begins, if you ask me.

I agree with that. What does it matter what Mike drinks? What does it matter whether he drinks or not? Mike would strengthen the Cabinet because he represents Breakages, Limited, the biggest industrial corporation in the country.

You hear that, sir. Your one supporter in the Cabinet admits that the industrial situation is too strong for her. I do not pretend to be able to control the women in my Cabinet; but not one of them dare support you.
I am afraid that that is only because the efficiency of the Post Office is as important to them as to the general public.
Stuff! They could get rid of me without shutting up the Post Office. They’re afraid of me﻿—of me, Amanda Postlethwaite.
You coax them, I am afraid.

Coax! What do you think they care for coaxing? They can have all the coaxing they want from younger and prettier women than I by paying for it. No use trying to coax that lot. Intimidate them: that’s the way to handle them.
But what can Amanda do that you cannot do?
I’ll tell you. She can’t mimic people. And she can’t sing funny songs. I can do both; and that﻿—with all respect, sir﻿—makes me the real queen of England.
If you provoke me, Bill, I’ll drive you out of your constituency inside of two months.
Ho! You will, will you? How?
Just as I drove the Chairman of Breakages out of my own constituency when he came down there and tried to take my seat from me.
I never quite understood why he turned tail. How did you do it?
She resumes her seat with triumphant self-satisfaction.
Should not the Queen support the King, your Majesty?
Sorry, sir; but there isn’t room for two monarchs in my realm. I am against you on principle because the talent for mimicry isn’t hereditary.
Now, anybody else? We have heard why the two ladies cannot support the King. Is there anybody who can?
I see that my appeal has been in vain. I do not reproach you, ladies and gentlemen, because I perceive that your situation is a difficult one. The question is how to change it.
Sign the ultimatum: that is how.
That’s the stuff to give him.
Gulp it down, sir. It won’t get any sweeter by keeping: what?
Oh, for God’s sake, sign, sir. This is torture to me.

I perceive, gentlemen, that I have come to the end of your patience. I will tax it no further: you have been very forbearing; and I thank you for it. I will say no more by way of discussion; but I must have until five o’clock this evening to consider my decision. At that hour, if I can find no other way out, I will sign without another word. Meanwhile, ladies and gentlemen, au revoir!
He rises. All rise. He marches out.
His last wriggle. Never mind: we have him safe enough. What about lunch? I am starving. Will you lunch with me, Lizzie.

Poor darling Lizzie! She’s a regular old true blue die hard. If only I had her brains and education! or if she had my variety talent! what a queen she’d make! Like old Queen Elizabeth, eh? Don’t grieve, Joe: I’ll lunch with you since you’re so pressing.
Come and lunch with me﻿—all of you.
What opulence! Can you afford it?
Breakages will pay. They have a standing account at the Ritz. Over five thousand a year, it comes to.
Right. Let us spoil the Egyptians.
Come on, come on: it’s ever so late.
Have you two been listening, may I ask?
Well, it would be rather inconvenient wouldn’t it, if we had to be told everything that passed?
Seating themselves at their writing tables and yawning prodigiously.

Orinthia’s boudoir at half-past fifteen on the same day. She is at her writing-table scribbling notes. She is romantically beautiful, and beautifully dressed. As the table is against the wall near a corner, with the other wall on her left, her back alone is visible from the middle of the room. The door is near the corner diagonally opposite. There is a large settee in the middle of the room.
The King enters and waits on the threshold.
I don’t want to see him.
How soon will you be disengaged?
I didn’t say I was engaged. Tell the king I don’t want to see him.
He comes in and seats himself on the settee.
What is our quarrel today, belovèd?
I have none when you are concerned. You must tell me.
She takes a book from the table and rises; then sweeps superbly forward to the settee and flings the book into his hands.
Looking at the title on the back of the book.
Songs of Our Great Great Grandparents
Opening the book and finding the page, his eye lighting up with recognition as he looks at it.
Read the first three words﻿—if you dare.
Smiling as he caresses the phrase.
The name you pretended to invent specially for me, the only women in the world for you. Picked up out of the rubbish basket in a secondhand bookseller’s! And I thought you were a poet!

Well, one poet may consecrate a name for another. Orinthia is a name full of magic for me. It could not be that if I had invented it myself. I heard it at a concert of ancient music when I was a child; and I have treasured it ever since.
You always have a pretty excuse. You are the King of liars and humbugs. You cannot understand how a falsehood like that wounds me.
Remorsefully, stretching out his arms towards her.
Put your hands in your pockets: they shall not touch me ever again.
Since when have you set up a heart? Did you buy that, too, secondhand?
I have something in me that winces when you are hurt﻿—or pretend to be.
Sitting down beside him, but beyond arm’s length.
I should like to kick you sometimes, when you are specially aggravating. But I shouldn’t do it well. I should be afraid of hurting you all the time.
I believe you would sign my death warrant without turning a hair.
That is true, in a way. It is wonderful how subtle your mind is, as far as it goes.
It does not go as far as yours, I suppose.

I don’t know. Our minds go together halfway. Whether it is that your mind stops there or else that the road forks, and you take the high road and I take the low road, I cannot say; but somehow after a certain point we lose one another.
And then you go back to your Amandas and Lysistratas: creatures whose idea of romance is a minister in love with a department, and whose bedside books are blue books.

They are not always thinking of some man or other. That is a rather desirable extension of their interests, in my opinion. If Lysistrata had a lover I should not be interested in him in the least; and she would bore me to distraction if she could talk of nothing else. But I am very much interested in her department. Her devotion to it gives us a topic of endless interest.
Well, go to her: I am not detaining you. But don’t tell her that I have nothing to talk about but men; for that is a lie; and you know it.
It is, as you say, a lie; and I know it. But I did not say it.
You implied it. You meant it. When those ridiculous political women are with us you talk to them all the time, and never say a word to me.

Nor you to me. We cannot talk to one another in public: we have nothing to say that could be said before other people. Yet we find enough to say to one another when we are alone together. Would you change that if you could?

Send all these stupid people packing. Make them do their drudgeries in their departments without bothering you about it, as you make your servants sweep the floors and dust the furniture. Live a really noble and beautiful life﻿—a kingly life﻿—with me. What you need to make you a real king is a real queen.
Oh, you are blind. You are worse than blind: you have low tastes. Heaven is offering you a rose; and you cling to a cabbage.
Why should I know it better than anyone else?

Why, because you have been married twice; and both your husbands have run away from you to much plainer and stupider women. When I begged your present husband to come back to court for a while for the sake of appearances he said no man could call his soul his own in the same house with you. And yet that man was utterly infatuated with your beauty when he married you. Your first husband actually forced a good wife to divorce him so that he might marry you; but before two years were out he went back to her and died in her arms, poor chap.

Shall I tell you why these men could not live with me? It was because I am a thoroughbred, and they were only hacks. They had nothing against me: I was perfectly faithful to them. I kept their houses beautifully: I fed them better than they had ever been fed in their lives. But because I was higher than they were, and greater, they could not stand the strain of trying to live up to me. So I let them go their way, poor wretches, back to their cabbages. Look at the old creature Ignatius is living with now! She gives you his real measure.
An excellent woman. Ignatius is quite happy with her. I never saw a man so changed.
It must be magnificent to have the consciousness of a goddess without ever doing a thing to justify it.
To me, who love beauty, yes. But you should hear the speeches Balbus makes about your pension.

And my debts: do not forget my debts, my mortgages, the bill of sale on my furniture, the thousands I have had from the moneylenders to save me from being sold up because I will not borrow from my friends. Lecture me again about them; but do not dare pretend that the people grudge me my pension. They glory in it, and in my extravagance, as you call it.
They would hardly have ventured on that without a hint from somebody. Was it from you?
You think me capable of that! You have a very low side to you, Magnus.

No doubt: like other mortal fabrics I have a wrong side and a right side. But it is no use your giving yourself airs, belovèdest. You are capable of anything. Do you deny that there was some suggestion of the kind?
How dare you challenge me to deny it? I never deny. Of course there was a suggestion of the kind.
Sublime! Nothing but genuine inspiration could give a woman such cheek.
But my wife? the queen? What is to become of my poor dear Jemima?
Oh, drown her: shoot her: tell your chauffeur to drive her into the Serpentine and leave her there. The woman makes you ridiculous.
I don’t think I should like that. And the public would think it ill-natured.
Oh, you know what I mean. Divorce her. Make her divorce you. It is quite easy. That was how Ronny married me. Everybody does it when they need a change.
But I can’t imagine what I should do without Jemima.
Nobody else can imagine what you do with her. But you need not do without her. You can see as much of her as you like when we are married. I shall not be jealous and make scenes.
That is very magnanimous of you. But I am afraid it does not settle the difficulty. Jemima would not think it right to keep up her present intimacy with me if I were married to you.
What a woman! Would she be in any worse position then than I am in now?
You mean, then, that you do not mind placing me in a position that you do not think good enough for her?
Orinthia: I did not place you in your present position. You placed yourself in it. I could not resist you. You gathered me like a daisy.
Did you want to resist me?
Oh no. I never resist temptation, because I have found that things that are bad for me do not tempt me.
Well, then, what are we talking about?
I forget. I think I was explaining the impossibility of my wife changing places with you.

I cannot make you understand: you see you have never been really married, though you have led two captives to the altar, and borne children to one of them. Being your husband is only a job for which one man will do as well as another, and which the last man holds subject to six months notice in the divorce court. Being my wife is something quite different. The smallest derogation to Jemima’s dignity would hit me like the lash of a whip across the face. About yours, somehow, I do not care a rap.
Nothing can derogate from my dignity: it is divine. Hers is only a convention: that is why you tremble when it is challenged.
Not a bit. It is because she is a part of my real workaday self. You belong to fairyland.
Suppose she dies! Will you die too?
Not immediately. I shall have to carry on as best I can without her, though the prospect terrifies me.
Might not carrying on without her include marrying me?
My dear Orinthia, I had rather marry the devil. Being a wife is not your job.
You think so because you have no imagination. And you don’t know me because I have never let you really possess me. I should make you more happy than any man has ever yet been on earth.
I defy you to make me more happy than our strangely innocent relations have already made me.
Your children are beautiful; but they are fairy children; and I have several very real ones already. A divorce would not sweep them out of the way of the fairies.
In short, when your golden moment comes﻿—when the gates of heaven open before you, you are afraid to come out of your pigsty.
If I am a pig, a pigsty is the proper place for me.

I cannot understand it. All men are fools and moral cowards when you come to know them. But you are less of a fool and less of a moral coward than any man I have ever known. You have almost the makings of a first rate woman in you. When I leave the earth and soar up to the regions which are my real eternal home, you can follow me: I can speak to you as I can speak to no one else; and you can say things to me that would just make your stupid wife cry. There is more of you in me than of any other man within my reach. There is more of me in you than of any other woman within your reach. We are meant for one another: it is written across the sky that you and I are queen and king. How can you hesitate? What attraction is there for you in your common healthy jolly lumps of children and your common housekeeper wife and the rabble of dowdies and upstarts and intriguers and clowns that think they are governing the country when they are only squabbling with you? Look again at me, man: again and again. Am I not worth a million such? Is not life with me as high above them as the sun is above the gutter?
She cannot restrain a gesture of triumph.

Some day perhaps Nature will graft the roses on the cabbages and make every woman as enchanting as you; and then what a glorious lark life will be! But at present, what I come here for is to enjoy talking to you like this when I need an hour’s respite from royalty: when my stupid wife has been worrying me, or my jolly lumps of children bothering me, or my turbulent Cabinet obstructing me: when, as the doctors say, what I need is a change. You see, my dear, there is no wife on earth so precious, no children so jolly, no Cabinet so tactful that it is impossible ever to get tired of them. Jemima has her limitations, as you have observed. And I have mine. Now if our limitations exactly corresponded I should never want to talk to anyone else; and neither would she. But as that never happens, we are like all other married couples: that is, there are subjects which can never be discussed between us because they are sore subjects. There are people we avoid mentioning to one another because one of us likes them and the other doesn’t. Not only individuals, but whole sorts of people. For instance, your sort. My wife doesn’t like your sort, doesn’t understand it, mistrusts and dreads it. Not without reason; for women like you are dangerous to wives. But I don’t dislike your sort: I understand it, being a little in that line myself. At all events I am not afraid of it; though the least allusion to it brings a cloud over my wife’s face. So when I want to talk freely about it I come and talk to you. And I take it she talks to friends of hers about people of whom she never talks to me. She has men friends from whom she can get some things that she cannot get from me. If she didn’t do so she would be limited by my limitations, which would end in her hating me. So I always do my best to make her men friends feel at home with us.
A model husband in a model household! And when the model household becomes a bore, I am the diversion.

Well, what more can you ask? Do not let us fall into the common mistake of expecting to become one flesh and one spirit. Every star has its own orbit; and between it and its nearest neighbor there is not only a powerful attraction but an infinite distance. When the attraction becomes stronger than the distance the two do not embrace: they crash together in ruin. We two also have our orbits, and must keep an infinite distance between us to avoid a disastrous collision. Keeping our distance is the whole secret of good manners; and without good manners human society is intolerable and impossible.
Would any other woman stand your sermons, and even like them?
What work have you that is more important than being with me?
Unfortunately, this silly business of government must be carried on. And there is a crisis this evening, as usual.

But the crisis is not until five: I heard all about it from Sempronius. Why do you encourage that greedy schemer Proteus? He humbugs you. He humbugs everybody. He even humbugs himself; and of course he humbugs that Cabinet which is a disgrace to you: it is like an overcrowded third class carriage. Why do you allow such riffraff to waste your time? After all, what are you paid for? To be a king: that is, to wipe your boots on common people.

Yes: but this king business, as the Americans call it, has got itself so mixed up with democracy that half the country expects me to wipe my perfectly polished boots on the Cabinet, and the other half expects me to let the Cabinet wipe its muddy boots on me. The Crisis at five o’clock is to decide which of us is to be the doormat.
And you will condescend to fight with Proteus for power?
Oh no: I never fight. But I sometimes win.
If you let yourself be beaten by that trickster and poseur, never dare to approach me again.
Proteus is a clever fellow: even on occasion a fine fellow. It would give me no satisfaction to beat him: I hate beating people. But there would be some innocent fun in outwitting him.
Magnus: you are a mollycoddle. If you were a real man you would just delight in beating him to a jelly.
Yes; but tea is at half-past four.
Catching him by the arm with a snakelike dart.
Impossible, belovèd. Jemima does not like to be kept waiting.
She pulls him back so vigorously that he falls into the seat beside her.
No, not today. Listen, Magnus. I have something very particular to say to you.
He tries to rise, but is pulled back.
Henpecked! What do you call this? At least my wife does not restrain me by bodily violence.
I will not be deserted for your old Dutch.
Listen, Orinthia. Don’t be absurd. You know I must go. Do be good.
He tries to rise; but she holds him back.
Do, do. It will be in all the papers tomorrow.
Panting but greatly pleased with herself.
She throws her hand up with a gesture of laughing defiance, and dances back to her seat at the writing-table.

Later in the afternoon. The Terrace of the Palace. A low balustrade separates it from the lawn. Terrace chairs in abundance, ranged along the balustrade. Some dining room chairs also, not ranged, but standing about as if they had just been occupied. The terrace is accessible from the lawn by a central flight of steps.

The King and Queen are sitting apart near the corners of the steps, the Queen to the King’s right. He is reading the evening paper: she is knitting. She has a little work table on her right, with a small gong on it.
Why did you tell them to leave the chairs when they took away the tea?
I shall receive the Cabinet here.
Well, I think the open air and the evening light will have a quieting effect on them. They cannot make speeches at me so easily as in a room.
Are you sure? When Robert asked Boanerges where he learnt to speak so beautifully, he said “In Hyde Park.”
Yes; but with a crowd to stimulate him.
Robert says you have tamed Boanerges.

No: I have not tamed him. I have taught him how to behave. I have to valet all the beginners; but that does not tame them: it teaches them how to use their strength instead of wasting it in making fools of themselves. So much the worse for me when I have to fight them.
You get no thanks for it. They think you are only humbugging them.
Well, so I am, in the elementary lessons. But when it comes to real business humbug is no use: they pick it up themselves too quickly.
No, sir. It’s the American ambassador.
No, ma’am. He is rather excited about something, I think. I can’t get anything out of him. He says he must see His Majesty at once.
Must!! An American must see the King at once, without an audience! Well!

What! When we still owe America that old war debt. And with a mad imperialist president like Bossfield! No you wouldn’t, my dear: you would be crawlingly civil to him, as I am going to be, confound him!
Tea! Who can think of tea at such a moment as this?

That is true, ma’am. I am just behaving like a crazy man. But you shall hear. You shall judge, and then you shall say whether I exaggerate the importance﻿—the immensity﻿—of an occasion that cannot be exaggerated.
Goodness gracious! Won’t you sit down?
Taking a chair and placing it between them.
You have some exciting news for us, apparently. Is it private or official?
Official, sir. No mistake about it. What I am going to tell you is authentic from the United States of America to the British Empire.
No, ma’am: you shall not go. Whatever may be the limits of your privileges as the consort of your sovereign, it is your right as an Englishwoman to learn what I have come here to communicate.
My dear Vanhattan, what the devil is the matter?
King Magnus: between your country and mine there is a debt.

Does that matter, now that our capitalists have invested so heavily in American concerns that after paying yourselves the interest on the debt you have to send us two thousand million dollars a year to balance the account.

King Magnus: for the moment, forget figures. Between your country and mine there is not only a debt but a frontier: the frontier that has on it not a single gun nor a single soldier, and across which the American citizen every day shakes the hand of the Canadian subject of your throne.
There is also the frontier of the ocean, which is somewhat more expensively defended at our joint expense by the League of Nations.
Rising to give his words more impressiveness.
Something even more wonderful than that has happened. One may say that the Atlantic Ocean has been submerged in the British Empire.
I think you had better tell us as succinctly as possible what has happened. Pray sit down.
There is a tradition to that effect.
No mere tradition, sir. An undoubted historical fact. In the eighteenth century﻿—
That is a long time ago.
Centuries count for but little in the lifetimes of great nations, sir. Let me recall the parable of the prodigal son.
It has. It has indeed, King Magnus.
Then what is it? I have not time to attend to the eighteenth century and the prodigal son at this moment.
I should like to see the faces of your Cabinet ministers, King Magnus, when they hear what I have to tell you.
So should I. But I am not in a position to tell it to them, because I don’t know what it is.
The prodigal, sir, has returned to his father’s house. Not poor, not hungry, not ragged, as of old. Oh no. This time he returns bringing with him the riches of the earth to the ancestral home.
He stares haggardly into futurity, now for the first time utterly at a loss.
Pulling himself together with a visible effort.
The rascal! Jemima: we shall have to live in Dublin. This is the end of England.

In a sense that may be so. But England will not perish. She will merge﻿—merge, sir﻿—into a bigger and brighter concern. Perhaps I should have mentioned that one of our conditions will be that you shall be Emperor. King may be good enough for this little island; but if we come in we shall require something grander.

I should be right sorry to contemplate such a reversion to a barbarous past. Fortunately, it’s impossible﻿—immpawsibl. The old warcry would not appeal to the cosmopolitan crews of the fleet of the League of Nations in the Atlantic. That fleet would blockade you, sir. And I fear we should be obliged to boycott you. The two thousand million dollars a year would stop.
But the continental Powers! Do you suppose they would consent for a moment to such a change in the balance of power?
Why not? The change would be only nominal.
Nominal! You call an amalgamation of the British Commonwealth with the United States a nominal change! What will France and Germany call it?
In what sense, may I ask?

Well, we find here everything we are accustomed to: our industrial products, our books, our plays, our sports, our Christian Science churches, our osteopaths, our movies and talkies. Put it in a small parcel and say our goods and our ideas. A political union with us will be just the official recognition of an already accomplished fact. A union of hearts, you might call it.
The United States, ma’am, have absorbed all the great national traditions, and blended them with their own glorious tradition of Freedom into something that is unique and universal.
We have a civilized culture which is peculiar to ourselves. It may not be better than yours; but it is different.

Well, is it? We found that culture enshrined in British material works of art: in the stately country homes of your nobility, in the cathedrals our common forefathers built as the country houses of God. What did you do with them? You sold them to us. I was brought up in the shade of Ely cathedral, the removal of which from the county of Cambridge to New Jersey was my dear old father’s first big professional job. The building which stands on its former site is a very fine one: in my opinion the best example of reinforced concrete of its period; but it was designed by an American architect, and built by the Synthetic Building Materials Trust, an international affair. Believe me, the English people, the real English people who take things as they come instead of reading books about them, will be more at home with us than they are with the old English notions which our tourists try to keep alive. When you find some country gentleman keeping up the old English customs at Christmas and so forth, who is he? An American who has bought the place. Your people get up the show for him because he pays for it, not because it is natural to them.
Well, can you blame them, ma’am? Look at the climate!
No: it is not the climate. It is the Horse Show.

I must think over this. I have known for years past that it was on the cards. When I was young, and under the influence of our family tradition, which of course never recognized the rebellion of the American colonies as valid, I actually dreamt of a reunited English speaking empire at the head of civilization.
Fine! Great! And now come true.
Not yet. Now that I am older and wiser I find the reality less attractive than the dream.
And is that all I am to report to the President, sir? He will be disappointed. I am a little taken aback, myself.
For the present, that is all. This may be a great idea﻿—
It may also be a trap in which England will perish.
How can we when we have not yet civilized ourselves? They have come to regard us as a mere tribe of redskins. England will be just a reservation.

Nonsense, dear! They know that we are their natural superiors. You can see it by the way their women behave at court. They really love and reverence royalty; while our English peeresses are hardly civil﻿—when they condescend to come at all.
Well, my dear, I do many things to please you that I should never do to please myself; and I suppose I shall end as American Emperor just to keep you amused.
I never desire anything that is not good for you, Magnus. You do not always know what is good for you.
Well, well, well, well! Have it your own way, dearest. Where are these infernal ministers? They’re late.
But the Princess told me I looked ridiculous in it!
That was very naughty of the Princess. You looked particularly well in it. However, you look well in anything. And now I leave you all to your labors.
Am I to be favored with the advice of my ministers on that subject?
By your Majesty’s leave, we will take the question of the ultimatum first.
Do you think the ultimatum will matter much when the capital of the British Commonwealth is shifted to Washington?
We’ll see it shifted to Melbourne or Montreal or Johannesburg first.
It would not stay there. It will stay at a real centre of gravity only.
We are agreed about that. If it shifts at all it will shift either west to Washington or east to Moscow.
Moscow thinks a lot of itself. But what has Moscow to teach us that we cannot teach ourselves? Moscow is built on English history, written in London by Karl Marx.
Are you inexorably determined to force this issue to its logical end? You know how unEnglish it is to do that?
I wish they had stayed there. I am English: every bone in my body.
God help England if she had no Scots to think for her!
What does the Cabinet say to that?
All their people came from Scotland or Ireland or Wales or Jerusalem or somewhere, sir. It is no use appealing to English sentiment here.
Politics are not suited to the English, if you ask me.
Then I, the only Englishman left in politics, apparently, am to be reduced to complete nullity?
The day for absolute monarchies is past. You think you can do without me; and I know that I cannot do without you. I decide, of course, in favor of a constitutional monarchy.
So! There is a catch in it, is there?
Not exactly a catch. But you have driven me to face the fact that I am unfitted to be a constitutional monarch. I am by nature incapable of the necessary self-effacement.
Well, that’s true, at all events. You and I are a pair, sir.

Thank you. Therefore, whilst accepting your constitutional principle without the slightest reserve, I cannot sign your ultimatum, because by doing so I should be making personal promises which I know I should break﻿—which in fact I must break because I have forces within me which your constitutional limits cannot hold in check.
How can you accept our principle if you don’t sign the ultimatum?
Oh, there is no difficulty about that. When an honest man finds himself incapable of discharging the duties of a public post, he resigns.
You might as well talk of beheading yourself. You can’t behead yourself.
Do not let us quarrel about words, gentlemen. I cannot resign. But I can abdicate.
They stare at him in consternation.
Whistling a descending minor scale very expressively.
Of course, abdicate. Lysistrata: you have been a teacher of history. You can assure your colleagues that there is nothing unprecedented in an abdication. The Emperor Charles the Fifth, for instance﻿—
You cannot abdicate except by my advice.
I am acting upon your advice.
Oh, come! Don’t be hard on the lad, sir. He has plenty of brains.

Oh yes, yes, yes: I did not mean that he is a nonentity: quite the contrary: he is much cleverer than I am. But I have never been able to induce him to take any interest in parliamentary politics. He prefers intellectual pursuits.
Don’t you believe it. He is up to his neck in business.
Just so. He asks me why I waste my time with you here pretending to govern the country when it is really governed by Breakages, Limited. And really I hardly know how to answer him.
Things are like that nowadays. My son says just the same.
Personally I get on very well with the Prince; but somehow I do not feel that he is interested in what I am doing.

He isn’t. He won’t interfere with you as long as you don’t interfere with him. Just the right king for us. Not pigheaded. Not meddlesome. Thinks that nothing we do matters a rap. What do you say, Joe?
After all, why not? if your Majesty is in earnest.
I assure you I am very much in earnest.

Well, I confess I did not foresee this turn of events. But I ought to have foreseen it. What your Majesty proposes is the straightforward, logical, intellectually honest solution of our difficulty. Consequently it is the last solution I could have expected in politics. But I reckoned without your Majesty’s character. The more I think of it the more clearly I see that you are right﻿—that you are taking the only course open to you.
I never said I was against it, Joe.
One king is no worse than another, is he?
Is he any better? The way you fellows scuttle backward and forward from one mind to another whenever Joe holds up his finger is disgusting. This is a Cabinet of sheep.
Well, give the flock a better lead if you can. Have you anything else to propose?
I don’t know that I have on the spur of the moment. We should have had notice of this. But I suppose the King must do as he thinks right.
Then the goat goes with the sheep; so that’s all right.
Who are you calling a goat?
If you come to that, who are you calling sheep?
There is nothing more to be said.
That means another half hour at least.
Woman: this is not the moment for your tomfooleries.
He rises and becomes the conventional House of Commons orator.
For my own part﻿—and I think I may speak for others here as well﻿—it has been no mere political tie, but a tie of sincere friendship.
Renewed murmurs of sympathy. Increasing emotion.
We have had our disagreements﻿—as which of us has not?﻿—but they have been family quarrels.
You’ll be the Vicar of Bray, Joe.
A joke’s a joke; but really﻿—
She has a perfect right to speak. You are a parcel of sentimental fools.
—he’s a jolly good fel‑low For he’s a jolly good fel‑low For he’s﻿—
Sudden silence and misgiving. They sit down furtively.
I thank you with all my heart; but there is a misapprehension. We are not taking leave of one another. I have no intention of withdrawing from an active part in politics.
You are looking on me, with an emotion which has deeply touched me, as a man with a political past. But I look on myself rather as a man with a political future. I have not yet told you my plans.
A retired king can’t have plans and a future.
Why not? I am looking forward to a most exciting and enjoyable time. As I shall of course dissolve parliament, the fun will begin with a general election.
Surely your expenses will be paid by the State.
Paid by the State! Is that all you know about electioneering in England?
You will get your whack out of the party funds, Bill; and if you can’t find the extras you must put up with straight votes. Go on, sir: we want to hear about those plans of yours.
My last act of royal authority will be to divest myself of all titles and dignities; so that I may step down at once into the position of a commoner.
Step up, you mean. The common man is the superior, not the inferior, of the titled man.
Not all of us would be capable of a sacrifice like that.
A fine gesture, sir. A fine gesture. I admit it.

There is no imposing on you, Prime Minister. The game is, of course, that when I come back into politics I shall be in a better position as a commoner than as a peer. I shall seek a parliamentary seat.
You in the House of Commons!
He’ll be at the top of the poll.
There won’t be any poll: it will be a walkover.
This shows what all your fine manners and friendly ways are worth.
I wish your Majesty every success.
Hear hear! Fair play, boys. Why shouldn’t he go into parliament with us?
Well said! well said! Why not?
They sit down in utter disgust.

There are several possibilities. I shall naturally endeavor to form a party. My son King Robert will have to call on some Party leader who can depend on the support of the House of Commons to form a Government. He may call on you. He may even call on me.
Breaks the glum silence by whistling a bar or two of the National Anthem.

Whatever happens, it will be a great relief to us to be able to speak out quite frankly about one another in public. You have never been able to tell the British people what you really think of me: no real criticism of the King is possible. I have never been able to speak my mind as to your various capacities and characters. All that reserve, that tedious affectation, that unwholesome concealment will end. I hope you look forward to our new footing as pleasurably as I do.
I am delighted, sir. You will fight Breakages for me.
Rising and speaking slowly, with his brows deeply knitted.
Produces it from his breast pocket and presents it to him.
With measured emphasis, after tearing the paper up into four pieces at two deliberate strokes, and throwing the pieces away.
He takes his hat from the balustrade and goes away through the park.
Rising reluctantly and taking his hat.
Can you really tear yourself away from politics?
Cheerful to the last as he, too, goes for his hat.

I shall bear it in mind. By the way, if you should happen to overtake the Prime Minister, will you be so good as to remind him that we quite forgot to settle that little affair of the proposal of America to annex the British Commonwealth.

They don’t take it in, Lizzie: not one bit. It is as if another planet were crashing into us. The kingdom and the power and the glory will pass from us and leave us naked, face to face with our real selves at last.

So much the better, if by our real selves you mean the old English stock that was unlike any other. Nowadays men all over the world are as much alike as hotel dinners. It’s no use pretending that the America of George Washington is going to swallow up the England of Queen Anne. The America of George Washington is as dead as Queen Anne. What they call an American is only a wop pretending to be a Pilgrim Father. He is no more Uncle Jonathan than you are John Bull.

Yes: we live in a world of wops, all melting into one another; and when all the frontiers are down London may be outvoted by Tennessee, and all the other places where we still madly teach our children the mentality of an eighteenth century village school.
Patting her consolingly on the back.
Now Magnus: it’s time to dress for dinner.
Going to him and taking his arm.
